_readme: Industry-agnostic digital marketing health check. 20 checks, five groups. Scores: 2 strong, 1 partial, 0 weak, na not applicable, null not run. Never score a check that was not run. applies_when is the default scope; where a check also carries a substantive rubric 'na' condition, the rubric na is the operative gate and must be decided during scoping, before results are seen. Values: always | local | advertises | publishes.

checks.title: Local pack presence
checks.question: Where does the business rank in the map pack across a grid around each of its own locations, for the terms a customer would type?
checks.command: run the grid actor with centerLat/centerLng/placeId from THIS location, not the city centre
checks.method: For each location, run a 5x5 or 7x7 grid centred on the location's own coordinates, with its place ID, for each money keyword. Record rank per point. Score the location, then roll up to the business.

rubric.2: In the top 3 at more than half the grid points, and never absent, across most keywords
rubric.1: In the top 3 at some points, or consistently ranked 4-10
rubric.0: Outside the top 3 at most points, or absent
rubric.na: No physical location serving walk-in or local-intent demand

checks.caveat: Rank is not revenue. A small-market top-3 can be worth less than a large-market rank 5. Also verify the listing matched is actually theirs; same-name profiles in nearby towns are a common false negative.

checks.title: Organic visibility for category terms
checks.question: Does a relevant page rank in the organic top 10 for the category terms a buyer would search, and is it the right page?
checks.command: query 'category + qualifier' per market; record position and landing URL
checks.method: Build the query list from how customers describe the need, not how the business describes itself. Check both position and whether the ranking URL is the page built for that intent.

rubric.2: Top 10 for most terms with the intended page ranking
rubric.1: Top 10 for some terms, or ranking with the wrong page (home page for a service query)
rubric.0: Outside the top 10 for most terms

checks.caveat: Run without personalisation and note the locale used. Results differ by device and geography.

checks.title: Branded versus non-branded dependency
checks.question: Is the business found because people already know its name, or because it wins category demand?
checks.tool: search results scraper, plus any public keyword source
checks.command: compare visibility for the business name against visibility for category terms
checks.method: A business that ranks first for its own name and nowhere for its category is harvesting demand it already had. That is a real asset, but it is not marketing performance, and it collapses when the founder or the brand-building stops.

rubric.2: Wins meaningful non-branded category visibility as well as branded
rubric.1: Mostly branded with a few category terms
rubric.0: Branded only
rubric.na: Pure referral or contract business with no search demand

checks.caveat: Strong brands make the phone ring while invisible for category search. Say which one you measured.

checks.title: Answer-engine readiness
checks.question: Can AI assistants read, understand and cite this business?
checks.command: fetch /llms.txt, /robots.txt, and parse schema.org JSON-LD on key pages
checks.method: Check for: an llms.txt; robots.txt not blocking AI crawlers; valid Organization/LocalBusiness schema with address, hours, services; FAQ or HowTo schema where relevant; content readable without JavaScript execution; clear semantic headings.

rubric.2: Schema complete and valid, AI crawlers permitted, content server-rendered, llms.txt present
rubric.1: Some schema, or crawlers permitted but structure thin
rubric.0: No usable structured data, or AI crawlers blocked, or content only renders client-side

checks.caveat: This is a readiness proxy, not proof of citation. It is the cheapest check here and the one most businesses fail outright.

checks.title: Indexation health
checks.question: Is what the business publishes actually eligible to be found?
checks.command: fetch sitemap.xml and robots.txt; sample URLs for status, canonical and noindex
checks.method: Compare sitemap URL count against what is reachable and indexable. Look for noindex on money pages, canonical tags pointing elsewhere, redirect chains, and orphaned location pages.

rubric.2: Sitemap current and accurate, money pages indexable, no blocking directives
rubric.1: Minor issues: stale sitemap entries, a few redirect chains
rubric.0: Money pages noindexed or canonicalised away, or no sitemap and poor internal linking

checks.caveat: Absence of a sitemap is not fatal on its own for a small site.

checks.title: Review volume and rating versus competitors
checks.question: How does the business compare on reviews to the competitors a customer sees beside it?
checks.command: pull the top competitors in the same category and radius, with review counts and ratings
checks.method: Absolute counts mean nothing without the comparison set. Compare against the businesses that actually appear in the same pack.

rubric.2: Review count and rating at or above the local median, and growing
rubric.1: Comparable rating but materially fewer reviews, or flat growth
rubric.0: Well below the set on count or rating
rubric.na: Category where reviews are not a buying signal

checks.caveat: Review counts accumulate over years; a newer business is not necessarily underperforming. Compare recent velocity as well as totals.

checks.title: Review response rate and latency
checks.question: Are reviews answered, and how fast?
checks.command: pull reviews with owner replies and timestamps; compute response rate and median latency
checks.method: Rate = share of reviews with an owner reply. Latency = median time from review to reply. Check negative reviews separately; those are the ones that matter.

rubric.2: Most reviews answered, median latency inside the stated or implied SLA, negatives answered fastest
rubric.1: Answered but slow, or negatives answered no faster than positives
rubric.0: Most reviews unanswered

checks.caveat: Edited reviews carry the edit date, which produces negative latencies. Drop non-positive latencies rather than letting them skew the median.

checks.title: Profile completeness and posting cadence
checks.question: Is the business profile fully populated and actively maintained?
checks.tool: places scraper with detail page enabled
checks.command: pull categories, hours, attributes, services, photos, posts and Q&A per location
checks.method: Check every location, not just the flagship. Empty satellite profiles are common and invisible from head office.

rubric.2: All locations complete, posting regularly, questions answered
rubric.1: Flagship complete, satellites thin, or posting sporadic
rubric.0: Incomplete profiles, no posts, unanswered questions, or missing listings

checks.caveat: Posting cadence is activity, not results. Score it as hygiene, never as performance.

checks.title: Publishing cadence
checks.question: How much is actually published, and how regularly?
checks.command: parse sitemap lastmod dates; bucket by month over the last 12 months
checks.method: Count published items per month from the sitemap rather than trusting a report. If a contracted volume is known, compare it.

rubric.2: Consistent cadence over 12 months, meeting any contracted volume
rubric.1: Irregular, or bursts followed by gaps
rubric.0: Little or nothing published in the last 6 months

checks.caveat: Cadence is the definition of activity, not quality. It exists to be compared against results, never quoted alone.

checks.title: Page uniqueness
checks.question: Are location and service pages genuinely written, or one template with the place name swapped?
checks.command: fetch comparable pages, strip boilerplate, compute pairwise similarity
checks.method: Compare location pages to each other and service pages to each other. High similarity across a set is city-swapping. Report the similarity figure so the claim is checkable.

rubric.2: Low similarity across the set; pages carry location or service specifics
rubric.1: Moderate similarity; shared skeleton with some genuine content
rubric.0: Near-identical pages differing only by name
rubric.na: Single page or no comparable set

checks.caveat: A shared template is not automatically bad. Judge the body copy, not the navigation and footer, and say what you stripped.

checks.title: Authorship and batch-publish signals
checks.question: Does the content look written by someone, or generated and dumped?
checks.command: parse article schema and page metadata for author, datePublished and modification times
checks.method: Look for: many items sharing one publish timestamp; generic authors such as 'admin'; no bylines; no author pages; identical structure across every post.

rubric.2: Named authors, staggered publish times, varied structure
rubric.1: Bylines missing or generic, but content otherwise varied
rubric.0: Batch timestamps, generic author, uniform structure across the set

checks.caveat: Batch publishing proves how it was uploaded, not who wrote it or whether it is any good. State it as a signal, not a verdict.

checks.title: Speed and Core Web Vitals
checks.question: Does the site load fast enough to keep the traffic it earns?
checks.tool: PageSpeed Insights API, run separately from the bundled collectors
checks.command: request mobile and desktop for the home page and one money page, then put the metric values in manual_results.json under W1
checks.method: Prefer field data where available; fall back to lab. Test a conversion page, not only the home page.

rubric.2: Core Web Vitals passing on mobile
rubric.1: Mixed, or passing on desktop only
rubric.0: Failing on mobile

checks.caveat: No bundled script calls PageSpeed Insights, so this check scores null on a bundled run and only carries a number once someone runs it and supplies the result. Lab scores vary run to run. Quote the metric values, not the headline score.

checks.title: Mobile experience
checks.question: Does the site work on a phone, where most of the traffic is?
checks.tool: HTTP fetch with mobile user agent, optional rendering
checks.command: check viewport meta, tap target sizing, and that a phone number is tappable
checks.method: Check the basics that break conversion: a tappable phone number, a form that fits, no interstitial covering the content.

rubric.2: Renders correctly, primary action reachable in one tap
rubric.1: Usable with friction
rubric.0: Broken layout, untappable contact, or blocking interstitial

checks.caveat: Automated checks miss visual breakage. Confirm with a rendered screenshot before making the claim.

checks.title: HTTPS and security headers
checks.question: Is the site served securely and kept current?
checks.command: inspect certificate, redirect chain and response headers; fingerprint CMS and plugin versions
checks.method: Check HTTPS enforced, certificate valid and not near expiry, HSTS present, and whether the CMS or its plugins advertise stale versions.

rubric.2: HTTPS enforced, current software, no version disclosure
rubric.1: HTTPS fine, software behind or versions disclosed
rubric.0: Mixed content, invalid or expiring certificate, or materially outdated software

checks.caveat: Version fingerprints can be spoofed or stripped by a proxy. Treat as indicative.

checks.title: Email authentication
checks.question: Is the domain protected so marketing email lands and the brand cannot be spoofed?
checks.command: query TXT for SPF and DMARC; probe common DKIM selectors
checks.method: Check SPF exists and is not overly permissive, DKIM is signing, and DMARC exists with an enforcing policy rather than p=none.

rubric.2: SPF and DKIM valid, DMARC at quarantine or reject
rubric.1: SPF and DKIM present, DMARC absent or p=none
rubric.0: No SPF or no DMARC at all

checks.caveat: The most reliably failed check in this set, and the easiest to fix. A domain that sends marketing email without it is carrying deliverability risk that nothing else in the programme can offset.

checks.title: Analytics installed and configured
checks.question: Is anyone measuring anything?
checks.command: detect analytics and tag manager containers across a sample of pages
checks.method: Check presence, and that it is on every page rather than the home page only. Note multiple or duplicate containers.

rubric.2: One analytics implementation, consistent across pages
rubric.1: Present but inconsistent, or duplicated
rubric.0: Absent, or only on some pages

checks.caveat: Presence of a tag does not mean goals or events are configured. You cannot see configuration from outside; say so.

checks.title: Conversion tracking
checks.question: Can the business tell which marketing produced a customer?
checks.command: look for call tracking numbers, dynamic number insertion, form handlers and event wiring
checks.method: Check whether phone numbers are tracked, whether the displayed number differs by source, and whether forms post somewhere that records attribution.

rubric.2: Calls and forms both tracked and attributable to source
rubric.1: One of the two tracked
rubric.0: Neither; the business is buying traffic it cannot attribute

checks.caveat: A header number differing from the tap-to-call link is a broken implementation, not a sophisticated one. Check both.

checks.title: Ad tags versus actual advertising
checks.question: Do the tags on the site match the advertising the business is actually running?
checks.tool: tag detection; public ad transparency libraries
checks.command: detect ad platform tags, then check the platforms' public ad libraries for live ads
checks.method: Two failure modes, both common. Paying for a channel with no tag on the site means spend nobody can measure. A tag with no ads running means a campaign stopped and nobody noticed.

rubric.2: Tags present and firing for every channel with live ads
rubric.1: Partial coverage
rubric.0: Advertising with no conversion tag, or tags for channels long dormant

checks.caveat: Ad libraries have uneven coverage by platform and country. Absence of a listed ad is weak evidence of no spend.

checks.title: Domain, DNS and hosting control
checks.question: What does DNS show about who runs this domain's infrastructure and who is authorised to send as it?
checks.command: resolve NS and MX, read the SPF record, and expand everything its include: and redirect= mechanisms resolve to
checks.method: DNS answers three questions and no others: which operator runs the nameservers, which operator runs mail, and how many third parties SPF authorises to send as the domain. Record the operator names and the sender list. Then ask the business which of those it recognises, because nothing in DNS distinguishes an operator the business runs from one a vendor runs on its behalf.

rubric.2: Nameservers and mail on operators the business names as its own, and every third party in the SPF record accounted for
rubric.1: Nameservers or mail run by a third party that is identifiable, or a short sender list the business can mostly account for
rubric.0: SPF is permissive, so senders are effectively unrestricted, or it authorises third parties nobody can account for

checks.caveat: DNS names the operator, not the owner. A business-run nameserver and a vendor-run one look identical in a lookup, so a 2 needs the business to confirm the list rather than the lookup to prove it; from DNS alone this check caps at 1. Registrant, registrar and expiry date are a separate manual sub-check: run a WHOIS lookup before claiming a domain is held by a vendor or close to expiry, because none of that is collected here. A privacy service hiding the registrant is legitimate and is not a finding. A stale SPF include outlives the contract that created it, routinely by years.

checks.title: Third-party and competing vendor tags
checks.question: Who else is already inside this website?
checks.command: enumerate every third-party script, pixel and container, and every authorised email sender
checks.method: Inventory what is firing. Look for two agencies' tags, abandoned vendor scripts still loading, and email platforms competing with the one the business says it uses.

rubric.2: Clean, coherent stack matching what the business says it uses
rubric.1: Some legacy tags still loading
rubric.0: Competing vendors live at once, or a stack that contradicts the stated arrangement

checks.caveat: For a buyer this is a diligence question as much as a marketing one. It shows who has access and what a transition would involve.
